title: Diaphragm
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 11.4 Axial Muscles of the Abdominal Wall and Thorax; 22.3 The Process of Breathing; 13.4; 23.3

main.t: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle between the chest and the abdomen: the main muscle of breathing.

simpler.t: The diaphragm is a dome of muscle under your lungs. It pulls air in when it tightens.

deeper.t: Its contraction flattens the dome, enlarging the thoracic cavity and lowering the pressure in the lungs.

facts.t: It separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Its upper surface is the floor of the chest.
Its muscle arises from the xiphoid process, the lower six ribs and cartilages, and the lumbar vertebrae.

simpler.t: It sits across the bottom of your rib cage, under your heart and lungs.

deeper.t: The pericardial sac and the parietal pleura fuse onto its central tendon.

items.name: Central tendon
items.t: The tendon in the middle of the dome, into which all the muscle fibres insert.

items.name: Caval opening
items.t: Lets the inferior vena cava pass from the abdomen to the thorax.

items.name: Oesophageal hiatus
items.t: Lets the oesophagus and its nerves pass into the abdomen.

items.name: Aortic hiatus
items.t: At the back: the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein pass through it.

simpler.t: It has a tendon in the middle and three openings for big tubes to pass through.

deeper.t: The three openings lie at about the levels of T8 (caval), T10 (oesophageal) and T12 (aortic).
deeper.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The vertebral levels of the diaphragm’s openings.

facts.t: Contracting, it moves down towards the abdomen and makes the thoracic cavity larger.
The lungs follow, because pleural fluid holds them to the chest wall. Their pressure falls and air flows in.
Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic lungs recoil.

simpler.t: Tighten it and air comes in. Relax it and air goes out by itself.

items.name: External intercostals
items.t: Work with the diaphragm in quiet inspiration, lifting the ribs up and out.

items.name: Abdominal muscles
items.t: With the diaphragm, they raise abdominal pressure in defecation, urination and childbirth.

items.name: Phrenic nerve
items.t: The phrenic nerve comes from the cervical plexus in the neck. It reaches the diaphragm at the base of the thorax.

items.name: Inferior vena cava and aorta
items.t: Pass through the caval opening and the aortic hiatus.

items.name: Oesophagus
items.t: Enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus.

simpler.t: The heart and lungs sit on it and the liver and stomach lie under it. A nerve from the neck works it.
simpler.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the liver and stomach lie directly under the diaphragm.

facts.t: The phrenic nerve comes from the neck (cervical plexus), a sign that the diaphragm’s muscle starts in the neck region.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The development of the diaphragm and why its nerve comes from the neck.

facts.t: A deep breath is mainly diaphragmatic; a shallow breath relies more on the intercostals (costal breathing).

items.injury: Damage to the pons or medulla, after a stroke or from drugs such as morphine.
items.damaged: The respiratory centres that drive the diaphragm.
items.cannotDo: Breathe regularly in sleep: breathing stops for short periods (central sleep apnoea).
items.why: Without signals from the centres, the diaphragm and intercostals do not contract.

items.injury: Part of the stomach slides up through the oesophageal hiatus (a hiatus hernia).
items.damaged: The oesophageal hiatus, which has widened.
items.cannotDo: Keep stomach acid out of the oesophagus: heartburn is worse lying down.
items.why: The hiatus no longer holds the junction of the oesophagus and stomach below the diaphragm.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Hiatus hernia and its symptoms.

items.q: Explain how contraction of the diaphragm draws air into the lungs.
model: The diaphragm moves down and the thoracic cavity enlarges.
Pleural fluid makes the lungs follow the chest wall.
Lung volume rises, so pressure in the alveoli falls below atmospheric.
Air flows down this pressure gradient into the lungs.
Quiet breathing: the diaphragm and external intercostals contract; expiration is passive.
Forced breathing: inspiration and expiration both use muscles.
Neck muscles such as the scalenes help forced inspiration.
Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.

items.q: Predict what happens to breathing if the phrenic nerve is cut on one side.
model: The phrenic nerve is the diaphragm’s motor nerve.
That half of the diaphragm cannot contract.
The intercostals and accessory muscles must do more of the work.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The effects of cutting one phrenic nerve.

check.stem: What passes through the aortic hiatus?
options: Aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein
check.why: The aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein pass through the aortic hiatus at the back.
The phrenic nerve, from the cervical plexus, connects to the diaphragm.

check.stem: What happens when the diaphragm contracts?
options: It moves inferiorly and the thoracic cavity enlarges
It moves superiorly and air is forced out
check.why: It moves down towards the abdomen, enlarging the thoracic cavity.
